title: Ibsen, associated with Baird’s, the stonecutter’s
html_source: The linking of Ibsen with the “stonecutters” leads Don Gifford to speculate that the allusion here is to Ibsen’s play When We Dead Awaken, appropriate for the state in which both men, but especially Bloom, find themselves, having been roused. The description of the sculptor’s wife’s feeling on being awakened in Ibsen’s play is appropriate at least for Bloom after his “awakening” to his true sense of himself as a Jewish man in Dublin after his experience in Circe: “Her airy freshness is as a breath of keen air. The sense of free, almost flamboyant, life, which is her chief note, counterbalances with the austerity of Irene and the dullness of Rubek.”
